He undertook the monumental task of creating a completely new alphabet, now known as Old Permic, specifically tailored to the sounds of the Komi language. Using this script, he translated portions of the liturgy and Scriptures. For this work, he was ordained a hierodeacon by Bishop Arsenius of Rostov, who blessed his linguistic and missionary preparations.

In 1379, fully prepared for his mission, Stephen traveled to Moscow to receive the blessing of the wider Church. He presented his case to Bishop Gerasimus, declaring, “I am resolved either to lead them to Christ, or to lay down my life for them and for Christ.” Moved by his conviction, the bishop blessed him, ordained him a hieromonk, and provided him with holy chrism, service books, and an antimension for celebrating the liturgy in the mission field.

Saint Stephen journeyed into the northern wilderness of Perm, living among people who worshiped idols, fire, water, and trees. He endured many hardships and sorrows as he began his work. He was particularly grieved by the veneration of a massive, ancient birch tree, which the Zyrians considered sacred and where they performed animal sacrifices. Stephen established his small cell not far from this pagan site, praying for an end to the superstition.

In a bold act of faith, Stephen set fire to the sacred birch tree to demonstrate the powerlessness of the pagan gods. The Zyrians were enraged and gathered to kill him for his sacrilege. The saint faced them calmly, asking them to judge for themselves. If their god had any power, he argued, would it not have been able to defend itself from a weak man and a small fire? This direct challenge forced the people to question their beliefs.

Following his challenge, Stephen preached about the one true Christian God, who is almighty, all-knowing, and full of goodness for those who love Him. Convinced by the destruction of the birch and the saint's powerful words, the newly-baptized Zyrians began destroying their own idols. On the very spot where the pagan tree had stood, Saint Stephen built the first church in Perm, dedicating it to the Archangel Michael, the vanquisher of the spirits of darkness.

Stephen’s mission was later challenged by a prominent shaman named Pama, who opposed the spread of Christianity. Pama entered into a public debate with the saint, boasting of his many gods who provided earthly bounty. After a long dispute, Pama proposed a trial by ordeal to determine which faith was true, challenging Stephen to walk with him through fire and water. Stephen humbly accepted, placing his trust entirely in the Christian God.

As the trial was about to begin, Pama was overcome with fear and begged the saint to save him from certain death. The people, seeing his cowardice, demanded that the deceiver be executed. Saint Stephen refused, stating, “Christ has not sent me to hand anyone over to death, but to teach.” Pama was banished, and Stephen’s meekness and mercy won over the population more effectively than any show of force, leading to more widespread conversions.

In 1383, Stephen’s tireless work was recognized, and he was consecrated as the first Bishop of Perm. Like a loving father to his flock, he built churches and monasteries, and established schools to train a native Zyrian clergy. He continued his translation work, providing the people with the Psalter and liturgical books in their own language. During a famine, he distributed bread and defended his people from corrupt officials, earning their trust as a protector.

Saint Stephen's spiritual stature was so great that in 1390, he and Saint Sergius of Radonezh are said to have spiritually greeted one another from a great distance. In 1396, while in Moscow on behalf of his flock, Saint Stephen reposed in the Lord. He was buried in the Kremlin, and his veneration as a saint began soon after his death. His life was recorded by Epiphanius the Wise, and he is remembered as a great apostle, enlightener, and a true father to the Komi people.
stephen-protomartyr: Saint Stephen is honored as the Protomartyr, the very first to shed his blood for Christ. A Hellenistic Jew and reportedly a kinsman of Saul of Tarsus, he was a member of the early Christian community in Jerusalem. His name, meaning "crown" in Greek, proved prophetic, as he was the first to receive the crown of martyrdom. He stands as the "starting point of the martyrs," a foundation for all who would confess Christ through suffering.

In the first days of the Church, a dispute arose concerning the daily distribution of food to the Greek-speaking widows. To resolve this, the Apostles appointed seven men "full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom" to oversee this charitable work. Stephen was the foremost among them, and this ministry became the foundation of the holy diaconate. For his leadership among this first group of deacons, he is revered with the title of Archdeacon.

Saint Stephen’s service extended far beyond administering charity. Scripture describes him as a man "full of faith and power," who worked great wonders and signs among the people. A powerful preacher of the Gospel, he engaged in debates with Jewish leaders. They were consistently unable to resist the profound wisdom and the power of the Holy Spirit with which he spoke, which only increased their hostility toward him.

Frustrated by their inability to defeat Stephen in debate, his opponents resorted to deceit. They secretly stirred up the people and bribed false witnesses to accuse him before the Sanhedrin, the Jewish high council. The fabricated charge was that Stephen had spoken blasphemous words against the Temple and the Law of Moses. This grave accusation set the stage for his trial and ultimate martyrdom for the truth.

As Saint Stephen stood before his accusers in the Sanhedrin, a divine sign was given to all present. The Holy Scripture records that everyone in the council looked intently at him and "saw his face as the face of an angel." This heavenly radiance, much like that of Moses after speaking with God, testified to his innocence and the presence of God's grace upon him. It was a silent, powerful witness to the truth he was about to proclaim.

Given the chance to defend himself, Stephen delivered a masterful oration, recounted in the Book of Acts. He traced the history of Israel, from Abraham to Solomon, reminding the council of God's constant guidance and miracles. He simultaneously highlighted a tragic pattern: Israel's repeated rebellion, idolatry, and persecution of the prophets whom God had sent. His speech was not a defense but a bold proclamation of salvation history and a condemnation of faithlessness.

The sermon reached its climax as Stephen directly confronted the council members, calling them "stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears," just like their ancestors who resisted the Holy Spirit. He accused them of betraying and murdering the Messiah, foretold by the prophets. As they gnashed their teeth in rage, Stephen, filled with the Spirit, gazed into heaven and declared, "Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!"

This heavenly vision was the final straw for his enraged accusers. Crying out and stopping their ears, they rushed upon him, dragged him outside the city, and began to stone him. As the stones struck him, the first martyr prayed with words echoing his Master's own from the Cross. He cried out, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit," and then, kneeling down, he prayed for his murderers, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them."

The martyrdom of Saint Stephen was a pivotal event with significant witnesses. Present and consenting to his death was a young man named Saul of Tarsus, who guarded the garments of the executioners and would later become the great Apostle Paul. According to holy tradition, the Most Holy Theotokos and the Apostle John the Theologian also stood on a nearby hill, watching the martyrdom of the first to die for her Son and praying for him.

After the stoning, the Protomartyr's body was left unburied, intended to be food for wild beasts. However, the respected Jewish teacher Gamaliel, who was a secret disciple of Christ, clandestinely sent his servants to retrieve the holy remains. He buried Saint Stephen with honor in a new tomb on his own estate near Jerusalem. Later, Gamaliel himself, his son Abibas, and the disciple Nikodemos would also be buried there.

For nearly four centuries, the location of Saint Stephen’s grave was unknown. Then, in the year 415, he appeared three times in a dream to a pious priest named Lucian, revealing where he and the others were buried. Following this revelation, the relics were solemnly unearthed and transferred to a church in Jerusalem. The uncovering was accompanied by miraculous signs, including an earthquake and a beautiful fragrance that filled the air.

The holy relics of Saint Stephen soon became a source of many healings. Around the year 428, they were solemnly translated from Jerusalem to Constantinople and enshrined in a church built in his honor. As the Protomartyr, he is commemorated by the Church on December 27, the third day of the Nativity feast, linking the joy of Christ's birth with the first holy witness to His divinity. His veneration also includes feast days marking the finding and translation of his relics.
stephen-the-great-of-moldavia: The Right-believing Voivode Stephen the Great was born around the year 1433 to Bogdan II, who would later rule the land of Moldavia. Stephen’s youth was marked by political turmoil and the constant threat of invasion. After his own father was assassinated, Stephen was forced into exile but never gave up his claim to the throne. With the help of his cousin, Prince Vlad of Wallachia, he returned in 1457, defeated his father’s murderer in battle, and was acclaimed by the people and anointed by the Church as the rightful ruler of Moldavia.

From the beginning of his reign, Prince Stephen was known for his deep piety and commitment to the Orthodox faith. He understood that his authority came from God and that his primary duty was to protect his Christian people and their ancestral lands. He was a man of prayer and frequent fasting, often seeking divine guidance before making important decisions or leading his army into battle. This profound faith was the bedrock upon which he built his 47-year reign, guiding his actions as both a statesman and a warrior.

Stephen’s rule was a near-constant struggle for survival, as Moldavia was surrounded by powerful empires. He fought dozens of battles to defend his principality’s independence and its Orthodox identity from the expansionist ambitions of the Ottoman Empire, the Kingdom of Poland, and the Kingdom of Hungary. For Stephen, these wars were not merely political; they were a sacred defense of the Cross against those who sought to conquer Christian lands. His courage and strategic brilliance earned him the respect of both his allies and his enemies.

He became known throughout Europe as a formidable “Champion of Christ.” This title was especially earned after the Battle of Vaslui in 1475, where his small Moldavian army won a miraculous and overwhelming victory against a massive invading Ottoman force. Following this feat, Pope Sixtus IV praised him as a true defender of the Christian faith. Stephen’s military prowess was seen by his people as a clear sign of God’s favor, inspiring them to persevere in the face of overwhelming odds and constant threats to their existence.

A beautiful and enduring tradition holds that Saint Stephen built a church or monastery after every battle. Whether in victory or defeat, he gave thanks to God or sought repentance by founding a holy place of worship. Through this pious practice, he is credited with constructing or restoring over forty churches and monasteries across Moldavia. These holy sites, many adorned with unique exterior frescoes, stand to this day as a testament to his unwavering faith and his desire to glorify God above all else.

Among the many monasteries he founded, the Putna Monastery held a special place in his heart. He designated this monastery to be his final resting place and endowed it generously, making it one of the most important spiritual, cultural, and artistic centers in the region. Voroneț Monastery, often called the “Sistine Chapel of the East” for its magnificent frescoes, was another of his famous foundations. Through his patronage, Saint Stephen ensured that the Orthodox faith would flourish and be passed down through generations.

Despite his many victories, his life was one of continuous sacrifice and struggle. In 1476, the Ottomans returned with an even larger army seeking revenge. At the Battle of Valea Albă, the Moldavians were defeated, and the country was ravaged. Yet, Saint Stephen managed to rally his forces and harass the invaders until they were forced to withdraw, preventing them from achieving a complete conquest. His resilience in the face of defeat demonstrated his unshakeable trust in God's ultimate providence.

As his long and arduous life drew to a close, the holy prince prepared his nation for the future. He gathered his son, Bogdan, and his council of nobles, giving them his final counsel. He urged them to remain steadfast in the Orthodox faith, to govern with justice, and to defend the country’s freedom. Above all, he warned them to never submit their Christian land to a foreign, non-believing power, but to trust in God and resist to the end.

Saint Stephen the Great reposed in the Lord on July 2, 1504, having ruled and defended his people for over 47 years. He was laid to rest at his beloved Putna Monastery, just as he had wished. From the moment of his burial, his tomb became a site of pilgrimage for the faithful. The people of Moldavia immediately recognized his sanctity, venerating him as a national protector and a holy man who had sacrificed everything for his land and his Lord, Jesus Christ.

For centuries, the memory of Stephen the Great was kept alive in the heart of the Romanian people. In formal recognition of his righteous life, his heroic defense of Christendom, and his role as a founder of churches, the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church officially glorified him as a saint in 1992. He is remembered as the Right-believing Voivode Stephen the Great and Holy, and his feast day is celebrated each year on July 2, the day of his holy repose.
suriel: Archangel Suriel is one of the seven holy Archangels who stand in the presence of God, eternally serving the Holy Trinity. His name, cherished in the Oriental Orthodox tradition, means “God is my Rock.” Before the creation of the visible world, God brought forth the bodiless heavenly hosts, and Suriel was created as a mighty prince among them. He belongs to the highest rank of angels known as Archangels, who serve as divine messengers and protectors of humanity, revealing God's mysteries and guiding us toward salvation.

As a chief of the heavenly hosts, Archangel Suriel’s primary duty is to execute God’s will and minister to those who are heirs of salvation. He stands with Saint Michael, Saint Gabriel, and the other Archangels before the throne of Glory, constantly offering praise and worship. The Church teaches that these great spiritual beings are appointed as overseers of nations and as personal guardians for Christians. Archangel Suriel participates in this sacred duty, watching over the faithful and defending them from spiritual dangers.

The name Suriel, meaning "God is my Rock," reveals the core of his ministry to humankind. This title signifies the unshakable strength, stability, and protection that come from God alone. Archangel Suriel embodies this divine steadfastness, acting as a spiritual anchor for believers who feel tossed about by the storms of life, temptation, and doubt. By invoking his name, the faithful call upon a powerful ally who helps them build their lives on the firm foundation of faith in Christ.

One of Archangel Suriel’s most important roles is that of an angel of repentance. Tradition holds that he is set over the spirits of people who have fallen into sin, gently guiding them toward true contrition. He inspires a holy sorrow for our transgressions and a deep longing for God’s forgiveness and mercy. Through his unseen ministry, he helps soften hardened hearts, encouraging souls to seek confession and return to the life-giving embrace of the Church.

Although not part of the primary canon for all Churches, the ancient Book of Enoch, which is part of the biblical canon of the Ethiopian Tewahedo Orthodox Church, names Suriel as a holy archangel. In this text, he is credited with a specific teaching role. He is the angel who revealed the course of the moon to the holy patriarch Enoch. This act demonstrates his role as an enlightener, sharing knowledge of God's perfectly ordered and wondrous creation with humanity.

In the Coptic Orthodox tradition, Archangel Suriel is especially beloved as the protector of the Holy Family during their flight into Egypt. When the infant Jesus, the Most Holy Theotokos, and Saint Joseph fled the tyranny of Herod, it is believed that Archangel Suriel appeared to them. He provided them with comfort in the desolate wilderness, guarded them against dangers, and guided their path to safety. This event highlights his tender and powerful care for the Lord and for all who are vulnerable.

The Archangel Suriel is also known as a powerful intercessor for healing. The faithful call upon him in times of sickness, asking him to carry their petitions for health to the throne of God, the ultimate Physician of our souls and bodies. His intercession brings comfort to the afflicted and strength to the weary, whether their suffering is physical or spiritual. Trusting in his prayers, believers find a firm "rock" of hope amidst infirmity, confident in God’s abundant mercy and healing power.

Archangel Suriel holds a solemn place in the Church’s understanding of the Last Things. Tradition teaches that he is one of the mighty Archangels who will sound the trumpet on the great and terrible Day of the Lord. This momentous task signifies his high authority and his role in the culmination of salvation history. His trumpet blast will announce the Second Coming of Christ and summon all of humanity, living and dead, to stand before the dread judgment seat for the final reckoning.

In holy iconography, Archangel Suriel is depicted as a majestic bodiless power, clothed in radiant vestments befitting his heavenly rank. He is often portrayed holding a censer, from which rises the sweet smoke of incense. This censer symbolizes the prayers of the faithful, which he gathers and presents as a pleasing offering before the throne of God. This image serves as a beautiful visual reminder of his vital role as a mediator of our prayers and a guide in our spiritual ascent.

The Church, especially within the Coptic and Ethiopian traditions, deeply venerates Archangel Suriel as a compassionate friend and powerful advocate for humanity. Believers turn to him in prayer for strength against temptation, guidance in their spiritual struggles, and for help in achieving sincere repentance. He is honored as a great protector whose presence brings peace and whose intercessions provide a steadfast defense against all evil, helping us to remain firm in our faith as if upon a rock.

The Coptic Orthodox Church specifically honors the holy Archangel Suriel with a feast day on the 27th of the Coptic month of Tobi. Additionally, he is commemorated with all the angelic hosts at the Synaxis of the Archangels, which is celebrated on the 22nd of the month of Kiahk. These commemorations invite the faithful to remember the constant and loving protection of the angels. Through his feasts, we celebrate Archangel Suriel's ministry and ask for his continued intercessions before our Lord, Jesus Christ.
susanna: Saint Susanna is honored by the Orthodox Church as one of the Holy Myrrh-bearing Women who faithfully followed and ministered to our Lord Jesus Christ. While her personal history is not detailed, her sacred role is recorded in the Gospel of Luke. Along with Joanna, Mary Magdalene, and others, she is named as a disciple who accompanied the Savior during His earthly ministry. Her presence in the Gospels highlights the vital part that devout women played in the life of Christ and the founding of His Church.

According to the Gospel, Susanna was among the women who had been healed by Christ of various infirmities or evil spirits. This personal, life-altering encounter with the Lord’s power and mercy filled her with profound gratitude and love. In response to this healing, she dedicated her life to following Him, leaving behind her former life to become a steadfast and loyal disciple. Her journey of faith was born from a direct experience of God's grace, which she never forgot.

As Christ and His twelve apostles traveled through the towns and villages of Galilee and Judea preaching the Kingdom of God, Susanna and the other women ministered to them. The Gospels state that they provided for the Lord and His disciples “out of their own means.” This humble and crucial service ensured that the material needs of the group were met, allowing Christ and the apostles to focus entirely on their mission of preaching, teaching, and healing the people.

Holy Tradition holds that the Myrrh-bearing Women, who had served Christ so faithfully during His public ministry, did not abandon Him during His Passion. While the Gospels do not list Susanna by name at the Crucifixion, the women who followed Him from Galilee are mentioned as watching His suffering from a distance. Their hearts were surely pierced with sorrow as they witnessed the crucifixion of their beloved Teacher and Lord, and they remained loyal even in His darkest hour.

After the Lord’s body was taken down from the Cross and hastily laid in the tomb of Joseph of Arimathea, the Sabbath began. Saint Susanna and the other women returned to their lodgings, their hearts heavy with grief. Observing the Sabbath rest as commanded, they lovingly prepared precious myrrh and aromatic spices. Their intention was to return to the tomb after the Sabbath had passed to give the Lord’s body a proper anointing, an final act of devotion and love.

In the deep darkness of early morning, on the first day of the week, Susanna and the other Myrrh-bearers set out for the garden tomb. As they walked, their love for Christ compelled them forward, yet they were troubled by a practical concern. They asked one another, “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” This heavy stone, sealed by the authorities, seemed an insurmountable obstacle, but their faith and devotion urged them onward.

Upon their arrival, the women were astonished to find that the massive stone had already been rolled away from the tomb’s entrance. Full of apprehension, they entered the sepulcher but did not find the body of their crucified Lord. Instead, they saw a wondrous sight: one or more angels, shining with a heavenly light, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain. Their initial grief and confusion quickly turned to fear and awe at this divine visitation.

The radiant angel spoke to the frightened women, bringing them comfort and announcing the most joyful news in all of human history. “Why do you seek the living among the dead?” the angel asked. “He is not here, but is risen! Remember how He told you, while He was still in Galilee, that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and on the third day rise again.”

Suddenly remembering the Lord’s words, the women were filled with an ineffable joy mixed with reverent fear. They departed quickly from the empty tomb and ran to find the apostles and the other disciples. In this act, Susanna and the Myrrh-bearers became the first evangelists of the Resurrection, the “Apostles to the Apostles.” Though the disciples at first disbelieved their report, the women courageously proclaimed the truth of what they had seen and heard.

Holy Tradition teaches that Saint Susanna, along with the other Myrrh-bearers, continued to serve the Lord after His Ascension and the descent of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. These faithful women remained central to the life of the early Church in Jerusalem. They likely assisted the apostles, supported the community of believers, and shared their firsthand testimony of Christ’s life, death, and glorious Resurrection with all who would listen.

The life of Saint Susanna serves as a powerful model of quiet faithfulness, profound gratitude, and courageous witness. Her story demonstrates that service to Christ can take many forms, from providing for material needs to being the first to proclaim the Gospel. She represents the countless faithful souls who serve God not for recognition or status, but purely out of love. Her steadfastness in the face of both sorrow and joy is an inspiration to all Christians.

The Orthodox Church venerates Saint Susanna as a holy and righteous disciple of the Lord. She is commemorated together with all the Holy Myrrh-bearing Women on the third Sunday of Pascha, a day known as the Sunday of the Myrrh-bearing Women. On this day, the Church honors their unwavering love, their courage at the tomb, and their essential role as the first witnesses to Christ's victory over death, reminding all believers to emulate their steadfast faith.
symeon-new-theologian: Saint Symeon the New Theologian (949–1022) is one of the most revered mystics and poets of the Orthodox Church. He is honored as one of only three figures in Orthodox tradition to be called a "Theologian," a title he shares with Saint John the Evangelist and Saint Gregory Nazianzen. This name was given in recognition of the profound depth and divine inspiration of his writings, which speak of a direct, personal experience of God.

Born into a noble family in the Byzantine Empire, the young Symeon was sent to Constantinople for his education. He entered service at the imperial court and seemed destined for a life of secular advancement and worldly success. However, his heart was not drawn to power or prestige, as he felt a deep calling to a different kind of life. A spiritual restlessness grew within him, preparing him for a radical change in his path.

The decisive turning point in Symeon’s life came when he met his spiritual father, the venerable elder Symeon the Studite. This holy monk, also known as Symeon the Pious, took the young man under his guidance and taught him the art of prayer. Through his elder’s instruction, Symeon had a profound and transformative experience of the divine, uncreated light of God. This vision of heavenly glory convinced him to forsake the world completely and dedicate his life to Christ.

Following this powerful spiritual awakening, Symeon entered the renowned Studite Monastery in Constantinople to live as a monk. He dedicated himself fully to the disciplines of prayer, fasting, and obedience under the watchful eye of his elder. After some time, he moved to the nearby Monastery of Saint Mamas, where he continued his intense ascetic struggle. His dedication and holiness were so evident that he was eventually chosen to become the abbot of the community.

Saint Symeon’s central teaching was a bold and passionate declaration for his time. He insisted that the direct, conscious experience of God's grace and uncreated light was not reserved for the apostles or saints of the distant past. Instead, he taught that this intimate union with God remains genuinely available to all baptized Christians who earnestly pursue a life of repentance, prayer, and ascetic effort. For Symeon, theology was not just theory but a living encounter.

To express the inexpressible, Saint Symeon became a brilliant poet and writer. In works like his "Hymns of Divine Love," he described his own mystical visions with astonishing candor and emotional intensity. His writings blend soaring poetry, profound theological insights, and practical spiritual instruction, creating a style almost unique in Byzantine literature. He spoke of the vision of Divine Light not as an abstract idea, but as a reality he had personally witnessed and experienced.

As abbot of Saint Mamas, Symeon sought to lead his monks toward the same experiential knowledge of God he had found. He enforced a strict discipline and encouraged his spiritual children to seek the Holy Spirit in a direct, personal way. However, his passionate intensity and uncompromising standards provoked resistance. Some monks, and eventually certain ecclesiastical authorities, grew uneasy with his claims and his style of leadership.

The conflict surrounding Saint Symeon intensified, particularly over his efforts to promote the formal veneration of his own spiritual father, Symeon the Studite, as a saint. This, combined with the challenging nature of his mystical teachings, led to official opposition. Ultimately, these tensions resulted in his trial and exile from Constantinople for several years. Despite this hardship, he continued to write and guide his followers from a distance.

Even in exile, Saint Symeon’s influence continued to grow, and he was later formally reconciled with Church authorities before his death. He reposed in the Lord in the year 1022. His theology of direct communion with God would profoundly influence later Orthodox spirituality, especially the hesychast movement championed by Saint Gregory Palamas. His life and work affirmed that the goal of Christian life is theosis, or deification, through the grace of God.

Today, Saint Symeon the New Theologian is venerated as a foundational pillar of Orthodox mystical theology. His hymnography and ascetical writings are treasured as among the most intimate and daring testimonies to the experience of God in the Christian East. The Church celebrates his feast day on March 12, though because this date often falls during Great Lent, the celebration is frequently transferred to another day to allow for a more joyous commemoration of his holy life.
symeon-of-emesa: Saint Symeon was born in the city of Edessa in Mesopotamia during the sixth century. From a young age, he shared a deep, brotherly bond with his friend, John. Living during the reign of Emperor Justin the Younger, the two were inseparable companions. This profound friendship would become the foundation for a shared spiritual journey that would lead them both to renounce the world and seek a life of radical devotion to God.

A pilgrimage to the Holy City of Jerusalem proved to be a life-altering experience for Symeon and John. As they walked in the footsteps of Christ and venerated the holy places, their hearts were set ablaze with divine love. This sacred journey moved them with an overwhelming desire to forsake worldly cares and attachments. They resolved together to dedicate the remainder of their lives to God through the rigorous path of monasticism, leaving everything behind for the sake of the Kingdom of Heaven.

Acting on their shared calling, Symeon and John sought out a monastery where they could begin their new life. They were welcomed by a venerable abbot named Nicon, who recognized their sincere desire for God. Under his guidance, they received the monastic tonsure, formally entering into the angelic way of life. They embraced the disciplines of prayer, fasting, and obedience with great zeal, beginning their ascetic struggle as brothers not only in friendship but now also in Christ.

Although they grew spiritually within the monastery, Symeon and John soon yearned for a more intense and solitary struggle. With their abbot’s blessing, they left the community to live as hermits in the harsh wilderness near the Dead Sea. This desolate landscape, sanctified by the struggles of countless ascetics before them, became their new home. Here, far from all worldly distractions, they committed themselves to a life of unceasing prayer and warfare against the passions, seeking God alone in the silence of the desert.

For more than thirty years, Symeon and John lived together in the desert, supporting one another through extreme asceticism. They maintained a discipline of silence, communicating more through prayer and shared purpose than with words. Through constant vigils, fasting, and spiritual warfare, they purified their hearts and minds, ascending to great heights of holiness. This long period of seclusion prepared them for the next stage of their service to God, equipping them with profound spiritual gifts and unwavering faith.

After three decades of seclusion, Saint Symeon achieved a state of profound dispassion and inner peace. It was then that God revealed a new and startling path for him. He felt called to leave the quiet of the desert and re-enter the bustling world, not as a hermit or preacher, but in a much more radical way. He informed his beloved friend John of his intention to feign madness for the salvation of others, a path that would require him to completely abandon his own reputation for the sake of the Gospel.

Saint Symeon traveled to the city of Emesa in Syria, where he began his extraordinary ministry as a "Fool for Christ." He intentionally acted in bizarre and shocking ways, behaving as though he had lost his mind. He would enter the city dragging a dead animal, overturn the tables of merchants, and eat in public with a lack of all decorum. The citizens of Emesa mocked, insulted, and ridiculed him, completely unaware that beneath this strange facade was a man of profound holiness and divine wisdom.

The purpose of Symeon's "foolishness" was twofold: to hide his spiritual gifts from the world to avoid praise, and to jolt people out of their spiritual complacency. By acting in a senseless manner, he exposed the vanity and foolishness of worldly values. While he endured scorn, he was secretly performing miracles, casting out demons, and offering spiritual healing. His scandalous behavior served as a unique and powerful sermon, saving many souls from sin by forcing them to look beyond superficial appearances.

While the world saw a madman, those with spiritual eyes perceived a great saint. In secret, Symeon would pray for the city all night, and his prayers had great power before God. He could see the hidden sins of others and would often expose them in a shocking way, not to shame the person, but to lead them to immediate repentance and humility. He possessed the gift of prophecy and offered profound, life-changing counsel to the few who sought his help, discerning his true identity as a vessel of the Holy Spirit.

After a life spent in hidden service, Saint Symeon reposed in the Lord around the year 570. His death was as humble as his life, and most of the city remained unaware of the great saint who had lived among them. It was only after his repose that his true holiness and the miracles he performed began to be revealed to the people of Emesa. By the providence of God, his faithful friend, Saint John, who had remained in the desert, also departed to the Lord soon after.

Saint Symeon's path of holy foolishness, known as "salos" in Greek, is one of the most difficult and rare forms of Christian asceticism. It is a powerful reminder of the Apostle Paul's teaching that "the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God." By embracing public shame and ridicule, Saint Symeon demonstrated the ultimate form of humility and self-denial. His life challenges us to seek God's approval rather than human praise and to recognize Christ in the most unexpected and humble of guises.

The Orthodox Church venerates Saint Symeon as a great wonder-worker and a profound model of selfless love. He reminds believers that sanctity is not always accompanied by outward piety but can be hidden beneath a cloak of humility and apparent madness. Saint Symeon the Fool for Christ is commemorated on July 21st, along with his spiritual brother and lifelong friend, Saint John. Their shared journey stands as a testament to holy friendship and diverse paths to the same heavenly Kingdom.
symeon-the-stylite-the-elder: Born around the year 390 in the village of Sis, located in the mountainous region between Cilicia and Syria, the future saint began his life as a humble shepherd. From a young age, however, his heart was drawn to God. He soon renounced his simple life in the fields to enter a monastery, dedicating himself completely to the path of spiritual discipline and prayer. This decision marked the beginning of a truly extraordinary life in service to Christ.

In the monastery, the young Symeon wholeheartedly embraced the ascetic life. He eagerly learned the ways of monastic discipline, engaging in prayer, fasting, and obedience with great zeal. He tried various kinds of spiritual practices, continually seeking to push the limits of his endurance for the sake of drawing closer to God. His dedication quickly set him apart as he prepared himself for an even more rigorous struggle in the wilderness.

After his time in the monastery, Symeon sought greater solitude in the wilderness to deepen his communion with God. As his reputation for holiness and severe asceticism grew, however, pious people began to flock to him in great numbers. They came seeking spiritual guidance, healing, or simply a blessing from the holy man. Many desired just to touch the hem of his garment, believing it carried the grace of God.

To escape the constant crowds and find the solitude he needed for uninterrupted prayer, Saint Symeon devised a novel form of asceticism. He was not motivated by pride or a desire for attention, but by a need to retreat from worldly distractions. He constructed a pillar, about ten feet high, and began to live atop it. This allowed him to be physically separate from the people below while still being a spiritual presence for them.

This new way of life, standing on a pillar (or 'style' in Greek), gave him the name 'Stylite.' Over time, as his fame continued to grow, he moved to progressively taller pillars to maintain his separation, with the last one reaching a height of about fifty feet. For more than forty years, Saint Symeon heroically persevered in this astonishing feat of devotion. He spent the greater part of his life standing upright in prayer between heaven and earth.

The saint's life on the pillar was a testament to his incredible endurance and love for God. He faced extreme weather, from the scorching sun to freezing winds, with unwavering resolve. He persevered in his upright stance even when one of his feet became gangrenous and other parts of his body gave way under the immense strain. His physical suffering was an offering of prayer and a spiritual battle fought for the salvation of the world.

From his high perch, Saint Symeon became a spiritual beacon for the entire world. The historian Theodoret of Cyrrhus, who witnessed his life, called him 'the great wonder of the world.' Multitudes of pilgrims journeyed from distant lands including Persia, Armenia, Georgia, Italy, Spain, Gaul, and even the British Isles, just to see the holy man. His radical devotion captivated the hearts of people from every walk of life.

God blessed Saint Symeon's unique struggle with abundant spiritual fruit. Through his powerful witness and prayers, thousands of nomadic Arabs were converted to Christianity and received baptism. His fame reached the highest levels of society; the King of Persia sent envoys to learn about his way of life, and the Queen humbly requested oil that had been blessed by the saint. He was truly an apostle to the nations from his pillar.

Saint Symeon was also a great champion of Orthodox doctrine. When many were being led astray by the heresy of Monophysitism, he used his influence to defend the truth. From his pillar, he confirmed the decisions of the Fourth Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon for many who were in doubt. His firm stand for the faith was instrumental in guiding many back to the Church, including the Empress Eudocia herself.

After a life of almost superhuman asceticism and unwavering service to God, Saint Symeon peacefully reposed in the year 459. He was sixty-nine years old, having spent more than four decades in his extraordinary ministry atop a pillar. His incredible example inspired a new form of monasticism, and other ascetics, like Saint Daniel the Stylite, would follow his path of becoming a 'stylite' for Christ, standing in prayer for the world.

The Holy Orthodox Church venerates Saint Symeon the Stylite as a great wonder of asceticism and a model of endurance. His life reminds the faithful that sincere love for God can take many forms, and that a life dedicated to prayer is a powerful witness. We commemorate this righteous father on September 1st, celebrating his unheard-of achievements and his unwavering defense of the true faith.
symeon-the-stylite-the-younger: Saint Symeon the Younger, also known as the New Stylite of the Wondrous Mountain, was born in the great city of Antioch in the 6th century. His father, John, was originally from Edessa, while his pious mother, Martha, was a native of Antioch. From his very conception, his life was marked by divine favor, setting him apart for a unique and arduous path of service to God. His parents raised him in faith, but his spiritual intensity would soon surpass all ordinary measures, pointing toward a life wholly dedicated to the Lord.

From his earliest childhood, Symeon lived a life of remarkable asceticism, demonstrating a spiritual maturity far beyond his years. Orthodox tradition holds that he was under the special protection and guidance of Saint John the Baptist, who prepared him for his future struggles. Instead of childhood games, Symeon was drawn to prayer, fasting, and solitude. This early devotion was a clear sign of his future calling to a life of extreme self-denial for the sake of Christ's kingdom and the salvation of his soul.

As a young man, Symeon formally dedicated his life to God by entering a monastery. This was a common path for those seeking to flee the world and pursue salvation with greater focus. Within the disciplined life of the community, he learned the foundations of monastic obedience, prayer, and spiritual warfare. This period served as essential training, strengthening his spirit and preparing him for the even more demanding and solitary ascetic feat that God had planned for him.

After his time in the monastery, Symeon felt a calling to a more radical form of asceticism. Following the example of the first great Saint Symeon, he ascended a pillar, becoming a 'stylite,' or pillar-dweller. For eighteen years, he lived atop this column, exposed to the elements and cut off from worldly comforts, dedicating every moment to prayer and contemplation. This incredible feat of endurance was only the beginning of his life-long struggle on a pillar, a living testament to his unwavering faith.

Following this long period, Symeon was guided by God to a new location which would become forever associated with his name: the Wondrous Mountain. Upon arriving, he did not immediately ascend a new pillar but first lived for ten years in a dry and rocky place. This time was spent in deep prayer and preparation, sanctifying the mountain with his ascetic presence. He was spiritually preparing the ground for his final and most lengthy struggle, turning the barren rock into a holy place.

Having completed his decade of preparation on the mountain's rocky ground, Saint Symeon began the final stage of his earthly asceticism. He mounted a second pillar, this one located on the Wondrous Mountain itself. He would remain on this pillar for an astonishing forty-five years, never descending until his death. This pillar became his fortress, his church, and his pulpit from which his silent example of prayer and endurance shone forth for the whole world to see.

Life on the pillar was a continuous spiritual battle and a testament to the power of God's grace. Saint Symeon endured immense physical hardships, including heat, cold, rain, and wind, with only the sky for a roof. Yet, in this state of extreme deprivation, he was granted profound spiritual gifts. The Lord counted him worthy of divine revelations and gave him the power to work many miracles, healing the sick and counseling the troubled who flocked to the base of his pillar.

Although he was physically separated from the world, Saint Symeon became a spiritual center for countless people. Pilgrims traveled from far and wide to the Wondrous Mountain to receive his blessing, ask for his prayers, and witness his holy life. His miracles and spiritual wisdom drew many to repentance and strengthened the faith of the Church. Through his extreme asceticism, he became a powerful preacher of the Gospel, showing that with God's help, the human spirit can triumph over the flesh.

Saint Symeon lived atop his pillar on the Wondrous Mountain until the end of his long life. He peacefully reposed in the Lord in the year 595 at the age of eighty-five. He had spent a total of seventy-nine years in direct and unceasing ascetic struggle, including sixty-three years living on pillars. His death was not an end but a glorious transition to the heavenly kingdom, for which he had labored his entire life with unmatched patience and love.

Saint Symeon is remembered as 'the Younger' or 'the New Stylite' to distinguish him from his great predecessor of the same name. His life of almost unbelievable asceticism, his miracles, and his divine wisdom made the Wondrous Mountain a place of pilgrimage for centuries. He stands as a powerful example of taking up one's cross and following Christ with absolute dedication. The Orthodox Church honors his memory and celebrates his feast day on May 24.
syncletica-alexandria: Saint Syncletica was born around the year 270 in Alexandria to a wealthy and distinguished family of Macedonian descent. She was both well-educated and very beautiful, attracting numerous suitors as she grew. From her youth, however, she felt a powerful calling to a different kind of life. She desired only to please God, choosing to dedicate herself to prayer and to preserve her purity as a bride of Christ.

Following the death of her parents, Syncletica took a decisive step to dedicate her life fully to God. She distributed her entire substantial inheritance to the poor, freeing herself from the cares and attachments of worldly wealth. This radical act of charity was a direct response to the Gospel, demonstrating her commitment to storing up treasure in heaven rather than on earth. By renouncing her fortune, she embraced a life of voluntary poverty for the sake of the Kingdom.

After giving away her possessions, Syncletica withdrew from the bustling city of Alexandria. Accompanied by her younger sister, who was blind, she took up a life of ascetic seclusion in an empty family tomb just outside the city. This crypt became their cell, a place where they could devote themselves entirely to unceasing prayer, fasting, and the unseen warfare against the passions, far from the world's distractions.

Although Amma Syncletica sought a hidden life, the fame of her holiness and profound spiritual discipline could not be contained. News of her ascetic labors spread quickly, inspiring many other devout women. Virgins and widows, drawn by her example, began to gather near her tomb. They longed to receive spiritual guidance from her and to learn how to live a life wholly consecrated to God.

At first, Syncletica was reluctant to become a spiritual guide, valuing her solitude and silence above all. However, she recognized God's will in the community that had formed and accepted her role as a spiritual mother, or "Amma." She began to zealously instruct the sisters who looked to her for guidance. Her teachings were powerful not only for their wisdom but because they were rooted in her own lived experience of ascetic struggle and communion with God.

Amma Syncletica's teachings, preserved in the Sayings of the Desert Fathers, shine with spiritual wisdom. She placed great emphasis on humility, warning that it is the foundation of all virtues. She taught that just as an uncovered treasure is quickly stolen, a virtue that is publicly displayed for praise is easily lost to vainglory. For this reason, she encouraged her disciples to practice their spiritual labors in secret, for the eyes of God alone.

The saint's wisdom focused on the battle within the heart rather than on outward appearances of piety. She cautioned against the spiritual peril of pride that can accompany even great ascetic achievements. She famously said, “If it is the season for fasting, do not dismiss fasting, claiming illness, for behold, even those who do not fast succumb to the same illness.” For her, the true goal of spiritual discipline was the purification of the soul from its passions.

In her eightieth year, after a long life of spiritual labor, God permitted Amma Syncletica to be tested by a grievous illness. She endured a painful affliction with remarkable Christian patience, viewing her suffering as her final contest and a form of martyrdom. She bore her intense ordeal without complaint, transforming her physical pain into a spiritual offering and an example of endurance for all the sisters who cared for her.

As her earthly life drew to a close, the holy mother was granted a divine vision. She saw holy angels and a choir of heavenly virgins who had come to escort her soul to the Lord, revealing to her the exact day of her departure. After providing final spiritual counsels to her weeping disciples, Amma Syncletica peacefully surrendered her soul to God around the year 350, entering into the joy of His Kingdom.

Venerable Syncletica is honored as one of the great Desert Mothers and a model for all who seek a life of prayer and interior discipline. She is one of the few female ascetics whose teachings were recorded in the celebrated *Apophthegmata Patrum*, or Sayings of the Desert Fathers. As a foundational figure of female monasticism, she is venerated as a saint in both the Oriental and Eastern Orthodox traditions, which celebrate her memory on January 5th.
tamar-of-georgia: In 1166, a daughter named Tamar was born to King George III and Queen Burdukhan of Georgia. As the king’s only child and heir, she was prepared for rule from a young age. When she turned twelve, her father proclaimed her co-ruler, an unprecedented move to secure her succession. For five years, the royal court served both father and daughter, as Tamar learned the duties of a monarch under her father's guidance, preparing to lead her nation.

Following her father's death in 1184, the nobility honored their vow and recognized the young Tamar as the sole ruler of all Georgia. At her enthronement, she became the first woman to rule Georgia in her own right. Because she was a reigning monarch and not a king's consort, the Georgian people honorifically called her "King" Tamar. This title was a testament to her supreme authority and the deep respect she commanded from her subjects.

One of Tamar’s first acts as queen was to convene a Church council to correct spiritual disorders in the kingdom. Exhibiting profound humility, she approached the bishops as if she were a commoner, honoring them as Angels of God. She exhorted them to “Judge according to righteousness... beginning with me,” and to allow neither wealth nor poverty to hinder their work. She saw her role as a divine service, promising to care for the souls entrusted to her by God.

The court arranged her first marriage to Prince Yuri, a valiant but deeply flawed man whose coarse character was unbefitting a royal consort. After his repeated immoral conduct, he was justly exiled from Georgia. Rejecting many other politically advantageous but personally unsuitable suitors, Tamar eventually agreed to a second marriage to secure the dynasty. She chose the noble Ossetian prince, Davit-Soslan Bagrationi, a descendant of Georgian kings, who became her faithful partner and a brilliant commander of her armies.

When a Muslim coalition led by Atabeg Abu Bakr threatened Georgia in 1195, Queen Tamar called her people to arms and to prayer. She instructed the faithful to hold vigils and give alms, while she herself inspired her troops, telling them to place their hope in God. Climbing a hill to the Metekhi Church in Tbilisi, she knelt barefoot before an icon of the Theotokos and prayed ceaselessly. Soon, the good news arrived: the Orthodox Georgian army had won a decisive victory at Shamkori.

Years later, around 1203, Sultan Rukn al-Din marched a vast army against Georgia, audaciously demanding that Tamar surrender and embrace Islam. The holy queen gave a firm reply, trusting not in armies but in “the right hand of the Almighty God and the infinite aid of the Cross.” Before the battle, she prayed barefoot before the Vardzia Icon of the Theotokos, then led her army to the city gates. Inspired by her unwavering faith, the Georgian soldiers routed the enemy at Basiani in a victory that resounded throughout the Christian world.

While she shone in royal finery by day, by night Tamar lived a life of strict asceticism, fasting, praying on her knees, and performing needlework for the poor. A vision revealed that a humble maidservant's throne in heaven was more glorious than her own, inspiring her to sew vestments for twelve priests. In another famous story of her piety, she grew distressed after believing she had ignored a beggar. In repentance for her distraction, she immediately offered her own precious jeweled belt to an icon of the Theotokos.

Saint Tamar’s reign is rightly called the Golden Age of Georgia, a period of unparalleled strength, culture, and faith. As ruler, she abolished the death penalty and all forms of bodily torture, famously calling herself the "father of orphans and the judge of widows." She commissioned the building of countless churches and monasteries, including the magnificent rock-hewn city of Vardzia. Her Christian charity was boundless, as she generously endowed holy sites not only in Georgia but also in Palestine, Cyprus, and on Mount Athos.

The peace and piety of Queen Tamar's reign created a flourishing of arts and literature. Great writers like St. John of Shavta composed hymns in her honor, celebrating her devotion. It was during this time that Georgia's national epic, Shota Rustaveli's "The Knight in the Panther's Skin," was written, a masterpiece reflecting the ideals of her court. Through countless legends, ballads, and songs, the Georgian people have immortalized her meekness, wisdom, and peace-loving nature, cementing her place as their most beloved ruler.

The holy queen’s life of intense prayer and secret asceticism eventually took a toll on her health. When she grew ill, the entire nation prayed for their beloved ruler, but God was ready to receive her into His Kingdom. After bidding farewell to her court and children, she surrendered her soul to the Lord in the year 1212. For her great faith, wise rule, and defense of Orthodoxy, the Holy Queen Tamar is venerated as a saint, with her main feast day celebrated by the Church on May 1.
tarasios: Saint Tarasios was born around the year 730 in the great city of Constantinople. He came from a very prominent and well-respected family, and his parents were known for their virtue and high social standing. From a young age, Tarasios received an excellent education, mastering both complex secular subjects and the sacred teachings of the Church. This combination of worldly wisdom and deep piety would prepare him for the incredible path God had chosen for him, a path that would lead him from the halls of imperial power to the throne of the Patriarch.

As a layman, Tarasios embarked on a distinguished career in the imperial court. He rose to the high rank of senator and served as the first imperial secretary, or 'asekretis,' for Emperor Constantine VI and his mother, the regent Empress Irene. In this powerful position, he was known for his wisdom, integrity, and just counsel. He navigated the complex world of Byzantine politics with grace, earning the respect of all, even as the Church around him was torn apart by the heresy of Iconoclasm, the destruction of holy images.

The patriarchal throne became vacant in 784 when Patriarch Paul IV, burdened by his past concessions to the iconoclasts, retired to a monastery. Before he passed away, he told Empress Irene that the only man capable of healing the Church was the layman Tarasios. When the Empress and the people called for him to become patriarch, Tarasios was shocked and humbly refused. He felt unworthy and pointed out that Church canons forbade a layman from being elevated so quickly to such a high office, especially without theological training.

Seeing the deep need of the Church and the persistence of the Empress and the people, Tarasios finally agreed to accept the patriarchal office, but only on one crucial condition. He insisted that a new Ecumenical Council must be convened to formally condemn the heresy of Iconoclasm and restore the proper veneration of holy icons. This was the only way, he believed, to achieve true peace and unity in the Church of Christ. His bold and faithful demand was accepted, setting the stage for a pivotal moment in Christian history.

With his condition met, Tarasios began his rapid journey into the clergy. He was tonsured a monk and then, in a short period, passed through all the necessary clerical ranks in succession: reader, subdeacon, deacon, and priest. Finally, on Christmas Day in the year 784, he was consecrated as the Patriarch of Constantinople. This layman who had served emperors now took on the awesome responsibility of shepherding Christ’s flock through one of its most turbulent periods, guided by his unwavering faith and love for the truth.

True to his word, Patriarch Tarasios immediately began working with Empress Irene to organize the council. An initial attempt to hold it in Constantinople in 786 was violently disrupted by soldiers who were still loyal to the iconoclast heresy. Undeterred, the council was successfully reconvened the following year, in 787, in the city of Nicaea, the same city that had hosted the First Ecumenical Council. With Saint Tarasios presiding, hundreds of bishops gathered to prayerfully examine the truth of the Orthodox faith concerning holy icons.

Under the wise and steadfast leadership of Saint Tarasios, the Seventh Ecumenical Council solemnly decreed the restoration of the veneration of holy icons. The Holy Fathers made a clear and vital distinction: we offer veneration and honor (proskynesis) to the saints depicted in the icons, but true worship (latreia) is due to God alone. By condemning Iconoclasm, the Council affirmed that icons are not idols but windows into heaven, honoring the Incarnation of Jesus Christ, who made the invisible God visible to humanity.

Saint Tarasios's struggles did not end with the Council. He later came into direct conflict with Emperor Constantine VI, who cast aside his lawful wife and demanded that the Patriarch bless his adulterous second marriage. The saint steadfastly refused to violate the Church's canons, enduring the emperor’s wrath and threats. He excommunicated the priest who illicitly performed the ceremony, proving that his loyalty was to Christ and His laws above any earthly ruler. His courage preserved the sanctity of Christian marriage and the moral authority of the Church.

Throughout his twenty-two years as Patriarch, Saint Tarasios was a true father to his people, especially the poor and suffering. He used his entire personal and patriarchal income for works of mercy. He built numerous hospitals, shelters, and homes for the elderly, the orphaned, and the destitute. He would personally visit these institutions, bringing comfort and aid to those in need. His life was a testament to the Gospel, combining a staunch defense of doctrine with profound and practical love for his neighbor.

Having guided the Church back to Orthodoxy and lived a life of holiness and charity, Saint Tarasios peacefully fell asleep in the Lord in the year 806. His passing was mourned by the entire city, which recognized him as a true man of God and a faithful shepherd. Miracles were soon reported at his tomb, confirming his sanctity in the eyes of the faithful. He is remembered as one of the great pillars of Orthodoxy, a wise hierarch who fearlessly defended the faith and lovingly cared for his flock.

Saint Tarasios was immediately glorified as a saint by the Church for his heroic defense of the faith against Iconoclasm and his shining example of a holy and compassionate life. His legacy is inseparable from the Triumph of Orthodoxy, which the Church celebrates annually on the first Sunday of Great Lent. On this day, we commemorate the victory over Iconoclasm that was secured by the council he led. The Church honors his memory as a confessor of the faith and asks for his holy intercessions before God.

The Orthodox Church celebrates the feast day of our Holy Father Tarasios, Patriarch of Constantinople, on February 25th. On this day, we give thanks to God for this great hierarch who combined the wisdom of a statesman with the humility of a monk and the courage of a confessor. Through his prayers, may we also hold fast to the true faith and show love and mercy to all those in need, venerating the holy icons as true windows into the Kingdom of Heaven.
tatiana-of-rome: The Holy Virgin Martyr Tatiana was born into an illustrious Roman family. Her father, a distinguished man who was elected consul three times, was secretly a Christian. He raised his daughter in piety, teaching her to be devoted to God and the Church from a young age. Tatiana grew up understanding the importance of faith over worldly status, preparing her heart for a life dedicated entirely to the Lord.

When she reached the age of maturity, Tatiana chose a life of perpetual virginity, betrothing herself to Christ as her heavenly Bridegroom. She disdained earthly riches and comforts, seeking instead the imperishable wealth of the Kingdom of Heaven. Because of her great piety and devotion, she was made a deaconess in one of the Roman churches. In this role, she served God faithfully through fasting and prayer, while also tending to the sick and helping the needy in her community.

This was a time of great trial for the Church in Rome. The city was ruled by the young Emperor Alexander Severus, but all power was truly held by the regent Ulpian, a cruel enemy and persecutor of Christians. Under his authority, Christian blood flowed like water throughout the empire. It was during this fierce persecution that the holy Tatiana was arrested for her faith and brought before the pagan authorities to be forced to renounce Christ.

Tatiana was first taken to the temple of Apollo and commanded to offer sacrifice to the idol. Instead of obeying, the holy virgin began to pray fervently to the one true God. In that moment, a powerful earthquake shook the ground, causing the idol to be smashed into pieces. Part of the temple then collapsed, crushing the pagan priests and many others who were present, while the demon that inhabited the idol was seen fleeing with a screech.

Enraged by this display of God's power, the tormentors tore out the saint’s eyes with hooks. Saint Tatiana bravely endured this agony, praying not for herself, but for her persecutors, asking the Lord to open their spiritual eyes. Her prayer was answered as the executioners suddenly saw four angels encircling the martyr and striking them. Eight of the men immediately believed in Christ, begged Tatiana's forgiveness, and were promptly martyred for their new faith.

The next day, Tatiana was again brought before the judge, who was shocked to see her completely healed and unharmed. They then stripped her, beat her, and slashed her body with razors, but a wondrous fragrance filled the air. The torturers became exhausted, claiming an invisible power was beating them with iron rods whenever they struck the saint. Indeed, angels were turning the blows back upon them, and nine more of the tormentors fell dead.

After being thrown in prison, Tatiana spent the whole night praying and singing praises to God with the angels. In the morning, she appeared before her captors even more radiant and beautiful than before. They then urged her to sacrifice to the goddess Diana, and she seemed to agree. However, upon entering the temple, Tatiana made the Sign of the Cross and prayed, and a deafening crash of thunder and lightning destroyed the idol, the sacrifices, and the pagan priests.

The martyr was then subjected to even more gruesome tortures, hung up and scraped with iron claws. Afterwards, they took her to the circus and released a hungry lion to devour her. Instead of attacking, the great beast meekly approached the saint and gently licked her feet. When they later threw her into a great fire, the flames did not harm her at all, showing that God's power protected her from every element.

Frustrated and confused, the pagans concluded that Tatiana must be a sorceress. Thinking her magical power was in her hair, they cut it off and then locked her in the temple of Zeus for two days. On the third day, the pagan priests entered the temple to offer a sacrifice. They were met with the sight of their idol shattered to pieces on the floor, and the holy martyr Tatiana joyfully praising the Lord Jesus Christ.

Having exhausted every form of torture and witnessing the powerlessness of their idols, the judge finally condemned the valiant sufferer to be beheaded. Saint Tatiana met her end with a spirit full of courage and faith. Her father, who had raised her to love Christ, was also arrested and executed with her. Together, they received their immortal crowns of glory in the Heavenly Kingdom around the year 225.

For centuries, the holy relics of Saint Tatiana have been a source of blessing for the faithful. Her honorable head was eventually brought to what is now Romania after the fall of Constantinople. After being kept in several holy monasteries, including Bucovat and the royal church at Curtea de Argeș, the precious relics found a permanent home. This journey reflects the deep veneration the Orthodox people have for the saint and her powerful intercessions.

Today, the holy relics of Saint Tatiana, including her honored head, are enshrined in the Metropolitan Cathedral of Saint Demetrios the Great Martyr in Craiova, Romania. The Orthodox Church celebrates her memory each year on January 12. Saint Tatiana is remembered as a heroic virgin who, despite having the fragile body of a woman, possessed a robust and valiant spirit, becoming a triumphant martyr for Christ and an inspiration to all Christians.
tekle-haymanot: St. Tekle Haymanot was born in the district of Zorare in Shewa, Ethiopia, to pious parents. His father was a priest named Sage Ze-Ab, and his mother was Egzi'e Haraya. For many years they were childless, but they prayed fervently to God for a son. The Archangel Michael appeared to them, announcing that they would be blessed with a child who would become a shining light for all of Ethiopia, guiding many to the path of righteousness.

From his youth, the saint, originally named Fisseha Tsion, showed remarkable piety and was filled with the Holy Spirit. A local pagan ruler named Motalami persecuted Christians and captured his father, but the young saint’s prayers brought about a miracle that saved him and converted the ruler. He was known for his love of prayer and Scripture, and his life was marked by divine signs that pointed to his holy calling and future ministry as a spiritual father for the nation.

Recognizing his spiritual maturity, the Coptic Metropolitan, Abba Kyrillos, ordained Fisseha Tsion as a deacon. Later, he was ordained a priest and given the name Tekle Haymanot, which means “Plant of the Faith.” He immediately began a powerful missionary work in his native Shewa, traveling from place to place to preach the Gospel. He confronted pagan practices and successfully converted countless people to the Christian faith through his inspired words and the grace of God that worked through him.

Desiring a deeper life of prayer and asceticism, St. Tekle Haymanot left his home to seek out the great monastic fathers of his time. He traveled to the monastery of St. Stephen on Lake Hayq, which was led by the renowned Abba Iyasus Mo'a. For nearly a decade, he lived there as a humble disciple, dedicating himself to fasting, prayer, and the study of monastic discipline, growing in virtue and preparing for the greater work God had planned for him.

After his time at Lake Hayq, the saint felt called to journey north to the ancient monasteries of Tigray, the cradle of Ethiopian Christianity. He visited holy sites and spent years at the famous cliff-top monastery of Debre Damo, living under the guidance of Abba Yohannes Kama. There, he embraced the most rigorous forms of asceticism practiced by the desert fathers, further strengthening his spirit and gaining a reputation for profound holiness and unwavering discipline among the monks.

Following his long period of spiritual formation in the north, St. Tekle Haymanot received a divine vision. The Archangel Michael appeared and instructed him to return to his homeland of Shewa. The Archangel revealed that it was God's will for him to become a great teacher and a spiritual father to multitudes, comparing him to the Apostle Paul. He was commanded to establish a new monastic community that would become a beacon of faith for the entire region.

Obedient to the heavenly command, St. Tekle Haymanot returned to Shewa and began preaching with immense spiritual authority. He eventually settled in a cave in an area known as Grarya, which would become the site for his famed monastery, Debre Libanos. Drawn by his holiness, powerful teachings, and the many miracles he performed, thousands of people flocked to him. Many chose to forsake the world and become his disciples, forming a vast spiritual army under his guidance.

St. Tekle Haymanot is renowned for his extraordinary ascetic labors, undertaken for the love of God and the salvation of souls. The most famous tradition of his life is that he stood in prayer for seven years on one leg. He endured this extreme penance until, according to his hagiography, his leg broke and withered away. This profound act of self-denial is seen as a symbol of his complete devotion and his spiritual victory over the flesh.

The saint's life was filled with supernatural signs and wonders granted by the Holy Spirit. He healed the sick, gave sight to the blind, and cast out unclean spirits through his powerful prayers. So great was his holiness that tradition holds he was given six wings, like the seraphim, to fly to Jerusalem to pray and to praise the Holy Trinity unceasingly. His miracles confirmed his apostolic mission and drew many to Christ.

After a long and fruitful life dedicated to serving God and his people, St. Tekle Haymanot reached the age of ninety-nine. Sensing his departure was near, he gathered his many spiritual children and gave them his final testament, encouraging them to remain steadfast in the Orthodox faith and in monastic discipline. He then peacefully commended his pure soul into the hands of God, leaving behind a legacy that would shape Ethiopian Christianity for centuries.

St. Tekle Haymanot is one of the most venerated and beloved saints of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. His monastery, Debre Libanos, grew into the largest and most influential monastic center in the nation, and its abbot held a position of great authority. The saint is often depicted in iconography with one leg, holding a cross and prayer beads, and with six wings, signifying his angelic life of unceasing prayer and service to God.

The Church honors the memory of St. Tekle Haymanot with several feast days throughout the year. His main feast day, commemorating his holy repose, is celebrated on the 24th of the Ethiopian month of Nahase (corresponding to August). Other feasts mark the day of his conception, his birth, and the translation of his sacred relics. To this day, the faithful seek his powerful intercessions for healing, protection, and spiritual guidance on their journey of faith.
tha-s-the-penitent: Saint Thaïs lived in Egypt and was famed throughout the land for her great beauty. Raised by her mother in a manner far from Christian piety, she fell into a dissolute life as a courtesan. Her fame was such that she led many men down a path of perdition, tempting them into sin and causing the ruin of their souls. Her story, however, would become not one of damnation, but of the profound and boundless mercy of God, Who desires the salvation of all.

Word of the sinful life of Thaïs eventually spread throughout Egypt, reaching the ears of the holy Abba Paphnutius. A great ascetic and disciple of Saint Anthony the Great, Paphnutius had converted many souls to the path of salvation through his own sanctity. Grieving for the spiritual harm Thaïs was causing to herself and others, the elder was moved by divine love and resolved, with God's help, to go to her and call her to repentance.

To approach the courtesan without causing alarm, Saint Paphnutius disguised himself in worldly attire. He traveled to the city where Thaïs lived and, finding her, presented her with a gold coin as if he intended to pay for her sinful company. Thinking he was just another client, Thaïs led the holy man into her private chamber. The elder went along with the pretense, for his goal was not to condemn her, but to awaken her conscience.

Once they were alone, Saint Paphnutius put a question to her, pretending to be afraid of being discovered. He asked if there was a more secret room where no one could see them. Thaïs replied that while they could easily hide from the eyes of other people, there was no place in the entire world where they could hide from God, for He sees everything. Hearing this, the elder knew that the spark of faith was not yet extinguished in her soul.

Seeing that she still possessed the fear of God, Saint Paphnutius revealed his true identity and purpose. He began to speak to her with the authority of a desert father, denouncing the grave sins she was committing. He vividly described the terrible and eternal judgment that awaited her, not only for her own actions but for all the souls she had corrupted and destroyed. His powerful words were not of anger, but of a deep and loving concern for her salvation.

The holy elder's words struck Thaïs’s soul like a bolt of lightning, and her conscience was fully awakened. She immediately burst into tears of profound and sincere repentance, realizing the depth of her fall. Without hesitation, she resolved to abandon her sinful life. As a first act of penance, she gathered all the gold, jewels, and rich clothing she had acquired through shame, carried them to the city square, and burned them all in a great fire for everyone to see.

Having renounced her past, Thaïs placed herself under the spiritual guidance of Saint Paphnutius. He led her to a convent and enclosed her in a small, isolated cell, instructing her to remain there in solitude and prayer. For three years, the former courtesan lived a life of the strictest penance, subsisting on only a little bread and water. She accepted this difficult enclosure as a just payment for the years she had spent in luxury and sin.

During her three years of seclusion, Thaïs did not feel worthy to speak the Lord’s name or recite formal prayers. Instead, she constantly turned her face toward the East and repeated one simple, heartfelt plea from the depths of her soul: “My Creator, have mercy on me!” This short prayer, offered with unceasing contrition and humility, became the constant cry of her heart as she sought forgiveness from the God she had offended for so long.

As her time of penance neared its end, Saint Paphnutius visited her. Thaïs confessed to him, “From the moment I entered this cell, all my sins have been constantly before my eyes, and I weep whenever I remember them.” The holy elder gave her great comfort with his reply, telling her, “It is for your tears, and not for the austerity of your seclusion, that the Lord has granted you mercy.” True repentance, he showed her, is born of a broken and contrite heart.

While Thaïs was still in her cell, another great ascetic, Saint Paul the Simple, was granted a vision from God. He was shown a magnificent throne in a beautiful dwelling in Paradise, prepared and waiting for someone. When Saint Paul asked who this glorious place was for, he was told that it was for the penitent Thaïs, whose sincere repentance and tears had been accepted by the merciful Lord. This vision confirmed that her struggles had found favor in heaven.

After three years had passed, Saint Paphnutius, assured of her forgiveness, brought Thaïs out of her seclusion. Having completely purified her soul with her unwavering penance, she was now prepared for eternal life. She soon fell ill, and after a brief sickness of only three days, she peacefully gave her sanctified soul to God around the year 340 A.D. The woman who was once a great sinner entered the Kingdom of God as a radiant saint.

The life of Saint Thaïs stands as a profound testament to the infinite mercy of God and the transformative power of repentance. Her story teaches us that no sinner is beyond hope, and that even a life steeped in darkness can be washed clean by sincere tears and a humble heart. She reminds us of the Lord’s words that publicans and harlots may enter the Kingdom of God before others. The Orthodox Church honors her as Saint Thaïs the Penitent, celebrating her memory on October 8th.
the-21-martyrs-of-libya: The Holy New Martyrs of Libya are a group of twenty-one courageous Christians who laid down their lives for their faith in 2015. Twenty of these men were Coptic Orthodox faithful from Egypt, and one was a Christian brother from Ghana. They were not theologians or clergy, but simple laborers who had traveled far from home to support their families. In their final moments, their profound faith transformed a violent act of terror into a glorious testimony of Christ’s victory over death.

Most of the martyrs hailed from the same area in the Minya Governorate of Upper Egypt, a region known for its strong Christian heritage and deep poverty. These men were fathers, sons, and brothers who undertook the difficult journey to Libya seeking employment. Their goal was humble and noble: to earn a living through honest work in construction and other trades in order to provide for their loved ones back home.

The journey to Libya was fraught with peril, as the country was engulfed in civil war and instability following its revolution. Extremist groups had gained power in certain regions, creating a dangerous environment, especially for Christians. Despite knowing the risks, these men placed their lives in God’s hands, driven by love for their families and the need to secure a future for them through their own hard labor.

In separate incidents during December 2014 and January 2015, the men were abducted by militants loyal to the Islamic State in the coastal city of Sirte. They were specifically targeted and separated from others because they were Christians. For many of them, their faith was visibly marked on their bodies by the traditional Coptic cross tattooed on their wrists, a sign of their identity in Christ.

During the weeks of their captivity, the martyrs were held and pressured to forsake their Lord, Jesus Christ.
