Freed from all earthly possessions, she began a life of homeless wandering through the poor districts of Saint Petersburg. She joyfully embraced her poverty, refusing all offers of help from her family and finding liberty in her lack of worldly attachments.

For a period of eight years, Saint Xenia vanished entirely from Saint Petersburg. It is traditionally believed that she spent this time on a long pilgrimage across Russia, seeking spiritual wisdom and instruction from holy elders and ascetics living in remote monasteries and hermitages. This hidden period of intense prayer and learning fortified her soul for the many decades of public ministry that would follow. She returned to the city spiritually strengthened and fully committed to her difficult path of foolishness for the Lord’s sake.

Upon her return to Saint Petersburg, Xenia took up her former life as a homeless wanderer, enduring daily ridicule with profound patience and prayer. While she seemed to wander aimlessly by day, her nights were dedicated to intense spiritual labor. She would go to a field outside the city and pray without ceasing until sunrise. It was also at night that she secretly carried heavy bricks to the construction site of a new church in the Smolensk Cemetery, astonishing the builders who found their walls mysteriously higher each morning.

Over time, the people of the city began to recognize that Xenia’s strangeness concealed great holiness and spiritual gifts. God granted her the gift of prophecy, and she often foretold future events, including the death of Empress Elizabeth and other matters affecting both the city and the imperial family. Her eccentric life was no longer dismissed as insanity but was increasingly revered as a powerful sign of God’s presence. She became known, against her own will, as a woman who was pleasing to God.

The citizens of Saint Petersburg came to love and revere Blessed Xenia. Shopkeepers considered a visit from her a guarantee of good business, while mothers rejoiced if she paused to kiss their child, believing her blessing would ensure a fortunate life for them. Though people often tried to give her alms, she would only accept the smallest coins, which she would immediately give away to other poor people. Her presence was seen as a holy benediction upon the city and its inhabitants.

After living for forty-five years as a fool for Christ following her husband's death, Blessed Xenia peacefully reposed in the Lord around the year 1803. She reached the age of seventy-one, having spent most of her life in radical poverty, constant prayer, and hidden acts of love for her neighbor. She was buried in the Smolensk Cemetery, the very place where she had labored secretly by night to help build the church. Her earthly journey of sorrow and self-denial had ended, but her heavenly role as an intercessor was just beginning.

Immediately following her repose, Saint Xenia's grave became a place of fervent prayer and pilgrimage. Faithful Christians flocked to her burial site, and so many took handfuls of earth from the mound as a blessing that it had to be refilled annually. When a heavy stone slab was later placed over her grave, it too was slowly chipped away and carried off by pilgrims over time. These acts of devotion were a testament to the countless miracles, healings, and answered prayers people received through her powerful intercession.

As veneration for the saint grew, a beautiful chapel was built over her grave in the Smolensk Cemetery, which remains one of Saint Petersburg’s most cherished holy sites. In formal recognition of her sanctity and the unending stream of miracles, Saint Xenia was officially glorified as a saint by the Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia in 1978. This was followed by her canonization by the Moscow Patriarchate in 1988. Her life of radical faith continues to inspire believers to look beyond worldly values to the Kingdom of Heaven.

The Orthodox Church commemorates Blessed Xenia of Saint Petersburg on January 24. To this day, Christians around the world turn to her in prayer with great love and trust. She is especially known as a powerful intercessor for those seeking employment, a home, a spouse, or help with marital and family difficulties. Her extraordinary life reminds the faithful that what the world deems foolishness can be the deepest wisdom in the eyes of God.
yared: Saint Yared was born in the city of Axum, Ethiopia, around the year 505 AD, during the golden age of the Axumite Empire. His parents, Abyud and Tawklia, were devout Christians who named him Yared, which means "descent" or "he who descended." From a young age, he was part of a faithful family, but his path to sainthood would begin with great personal struggle. His early life set the stage for a divine intervention that would forever change the worship of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.

After the early death of his father, Yared’s mother entrusted his education to her brother, a priest named Gedewon. Yared was a poor student who found it exceptionally difficult to learn the Psalms and liturgical chants. Frustrated by his lack of progress, his uncle disciplined him harshly, and Yared often felt discouraged and ashamed. Unable to succeed through his own efforts, he felt like a failure and eventually ran away from his uncle’s school, despairing of his future.

While wandering in the wilderness, disheartened and alone, Yared sought shelter under a tree. There, he watched a small caterpillar repeatedly try to climb the trunk of the tree. It fell down again and again, but with great persistence, it finally reached a leaf. This simple act of nature was a profound lesson for Yared. He realized that if a creature could achieve its goal through perseverance, then he, with God’s help, could also overcome his own struggles.

Inspired by the caterpillar's persistence, Yared returned to his studies with renewed determination and turned to fervent prayer. He asked God for wisdom and an open heart to learn. According to sacred tradition, God answered his prayer in a miraculous way. He sent three birds from paradise which, in a divine vision, lifted Yared up to the heavenly Jerusalem. There, he heard the angelic choirs and was taught the sublime melodies of praise sung before the throne of God.

When Yared returned from his heavenly vision, he was a changed man, filled with the Holy Spirit and a divine musical gift. He went to the main church in Axum and began to sing the holy melodies he had learned in heaven. These chants, which he called 'Zema,' were organized into three distinct modes: Ge’ez, Ezel, and Araray. These modes reflect different aspects of the liturgy—praise, sorrow, and contemplation—and form the very foundation of Ethiopian sacred music.

The beautiful and heavenly music of Saint Yared soon reached the ears of the pious Emperor Gebre Meskel. The emperor was deeply moved by the chants and recognized their divine origin. He became a devoted patron of Yared, bringing him to the imperial court to serve as the chief musician of the cathedral in Axum. With royal support, Yared dedicated himself to composing and teaching, creating a complete system of liturgical music for the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.

The power of Yared's music was so profound that it transported listeners into a state of spiritual ecstasy. On one occasion, while Yared was chanting hymns for the Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, Emperor Gebre Meskel stood beside him, completely entranced. The emperor leaned on his spear, and without realizing it, he accidentally pierced Yared’s foot. So absorbed were they both in the holy music that neither noticed the injury until the chant was over.

When the emperor saw the blood on the floor and realized what he had done, he was filled with remorse. He begged Yared for forgiveness and offered to grant him any wish as compensation for the wound. Yared, however, had no desire for worldly riches or status. Instead, he made a humble request: to be released from his duties at the court so that he could retreat from the world and live as a hermit, dedicating his remaining years entirely to prayer and asceticism.

Though saddened to lose his presence at court, the emperor honored Yared's pious wish. The saint traveled to the rugged Semien Mountains, seeking solitude to draw closer to God. In this remote wilderness, he lived a life of intense prayer, fasting, and spiritual struggle. He continued his holy work, composing hymns and writing his masterwork, the "Deggwa," a comprehensive book of chants for the entire church year, which remains an essential text for the Ethiopian Church.

Saint Yared’s legacy is immeasurable. He is not only credited with creating the rich and complex system of Ethiopian liturgical chant but also with developing one of the world's earliest systems of musical notation to preserve it. These notations, using signs and symbols, ensured that the divine melodies could be passed down accurately through generations. His work provided the Ethiopian Church with a unique and sacred musical identity that is still a central part of its worship today.

The end of Saint Yared's earthly life is shrouded in holy mystery. According to the tradition of the Ethiopian Church, he did not die but was taken directly into heaven from his hermitage in the Semien Mountains, similar to the Prophet Enoch and the Prophet Elijah. He disappeared while in deep prayer and communion with God, leaving behind his precious writings and musical instruments as a testament to his holy life. He is forever remembered as a heavenly musician on earth.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church honors Saint Yared as one of its most important and beloved saints. He is venerated as a theologian, a poet, and the father of sacred music, whose Zema chants are considered prayers in their own right. The faithful celebrate his feast day annually on Genbot 11 (May 19 in the Gregorian calendar), remembering the man who brought the melodies of heaven down to earth to glorify God and edify His Church.
zacchaeus: Before his life-changing encounter with Christ, Saint Zacchaeus was a well-known figure in the city of Jericho. As a chief tax collector, or publican, he had amassed considerable wealth by working for the occupying Roman government. This profession was widely despised, as tax collectors were often corrupt and extorted money from their own people, making them outcasts in Jewish society. Consequently, Zacchaeus was viewed by his neighbors not just as a wealthy man, but as a prominent sinner.

When Jesus Christ passed through Jericho, a great crowd gathered to see the famed teacher and miracle-worker. Zacchaeus, too, was filled with an intense desire to see who Jesus was, a yearning that marked the beginning of his salvation. However, a significant obstacle stood in his way: the Gospels tell us he was a man of short stature. The dense crowd of people taller than him completely blocked his view, making it impossible for him to catch even a glimpse of the Lord.

Unwilling to be deterred, Zacchaeus demonstrated remarkable humility and determination. He put aside the dignity of his wealthy status and ran ahead of the procession. Spying a sycamore tree along the path where Jesus would pass, he climbed up into its branches to get a clear view. This simple act of climbing a tree revealed the earnestness of his heart and has become a powerful symbol for us, showing how we must overcome our own spiritual shortness and sin to seek the Lord.

As the Lord approached the spot, He stopped, looked directly up into the branches, and called out to the tax collector by name. “Zacchaeus,” Jesus said, “make haste and come down, for today I must stay at your house.” This was a stunning moment; Christ did not wait for Zacchaeus to approach Him but initiated the encounter Himself. By seeking out the sinner and inviting Himself into his home, Jesus revealed the depth of God’s personal and pursuing love for every soul.

Zacchaeus immediately scrambled down from the tree and received the Lord into his home with tremendous joy. His happiness stood in stark contrast to the reaction of the crowd, who began to grumble and complain. They murmured among themselves that Jesus had gone to be the guest of a man who was a sinner, failing to understand the divine mercy at work. This scene highlights the difference between God’s loving compassion and rigid human judgment.

In the presence of the Lord, Zacchaeus’s heart was completely transformed, and he immediately demonstrated the fruits of true repentance. He stood and declared, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken anything from anyone by false accusation, I restore it fourfold.” This promise went far beyond the requirements of the Law, proving the sincerity of his conversion and his desire to make amends for his past sins.

Seeing the profound change in Zacchaeus, Jesus announced to all who were present, “Today salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham.” With these words, Christ affirmed that Zacchaeus’s repentance had restored him to the community of faith. The Lord then declared His own mission, saying, “for the Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost,” perfectly summarizing the beautiful miracle of conversion they had all just witnessed.

The grace that Zacchaeus received that day continued to work in him for the rest of his life. After the Lord’s glorious Ascension into heaven, Zacchaeus did not return to his former life of wealth and corruption. Instead, filled with the Holy Spirit, he became a devoted follower of Christ and a member of the early Church. His life stands as a testament to the fact that a single, genuine encounter with the Lord can completely reorient a person’s existence toward holiness and service.

According to holy Orthodox tradition, the repentant tax collector became a disciple and companion of the Holy Apostles. He is believed to have traveled with Saint Peter, the chief of the Apostles, on his missionary journeys. Having been personally sought out and saved by Christ, Zacchaeus dedicated his new life to spreading the same message of salvation he had received. He helped to establish the Church and bring others from darkness into the light of the Gospel.

In recognition of his faithfulness and apostolic zeal, Saint Peter eventually consecrated Zacchaeus as the first bishop of the city of Caesarea in Palestine. In this sacred office, he became a spiritual father to his flock, guiding the Christian community with wisdom and love. The man who once took from others now gave himself completely to the service of God and His people, shepherding the Church and preserving the holy faith passed down from Christ.

Saint Zacchaeus served the Lord faithfully as a bishop for the remainder of his days, living out the repentance he professed in his home in Jericho. Having completed his earthly course, he reposed peacefully in the Lord. The Church honors him as one of the Apostles and a shining example of how God’s mercy can transform a sinner into a saint. His story assures us that no one is beyond the reach of God’s saving love.

The Orthodox Church commemorates the Holy Apostle Zacchaeus on April 20. Liturgically, his story holds a special place in the preparation for Great Lent. The Gospel of his calling is read on the Sunday of Zacchaeus, which signals the approach of the Lenten season. His example encourages us to begin our own spiritual journey by acknowledging our sinfulness and making the effort, like him, to seek and receive Jesus into our hearts and homes.
zacharias: The Holy and Righteous Prophet Zacharias was a priest of the Old Covenant and the father of the glorious Prophet, Forerunner, and Baptist, John. He was a descendant of Aaron, from the priestly lineage of Abia, and his father’s name was Barachias. Zacharias served God faithfully in the Temple at Jerusalem, holding the eighth order of service. His life was marked by piety and a deep commitment to the Law of the Lord, setting a righteous example for all of Israel as he awaited the fulfillment of God’s promises.

Zacharias was married to the Righteous Elizabeth, who was also of the lineage of Aaron. According to tradition, Elizabeth’s mother, Sophia, was the sister of Saint Anna, the mother of the Most Holy Theotokos, making Elizabeth a kinswoman of the Virgin Mary. Both Zacharias and Elizabeth were devout and walked blamelessly in all the commandments of the Lord. However, they were advanced in years and had no children, a reality that brought them great sorrow and was considered a reproach among the people of their time.

One day, while it was his turn to serve, Zacharias entered the sanctuary of the Temple to offer incense. As the people prayed outside, the Archangel Gabriel suddenly appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar. Seeing the heavenly messenger, Zacharias was filled with fear and great confusion. But the Archangel spoke to him with comforting words, saying, “Fear not, Zacharias,” preparing him to receive a message of immense joy that would change not only his life but the course of salvation history.

The Archangel Gabriel announced that the long-standing prayers of Zacharias and Elizabeth had been answered. He promised that Elizabeth would conceive and bear a son, and they were to name him John. Gabriel prophesied that this child would be great in the sight of the Lord, filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother's womb. He would turn many of the children of Israel back to God and go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah to make ready a people prepared for Him.

Hearing this incredible news, Zacharias questioned the Archangel. He found it difficult to believe the promise, given that both he and his wife were very old. In response to his doubt, the angel revealed his identity: “I am Gabriel, who stand in the presence of God.” As a sign of the truth of his words and as a gentle rebuke for his wavering faith, Gabriel declared that Zacharias would be struck dumb and unable to speak until the day the child was born.

Zacharias returned home, unable to speak, and his wife Elizabeth miraculously conceived as the angel had foretold. After her months of pregnancy were completed, she gave birth to a son. On the eighth day, the day of circumcision, friends and relatives gathered, assuming the child would be named Zacharias after his father. But Elizabeth, guided by the Holy Spirit, firmly stated, "No; he shall be called John," surprising everyone, as no one in their family had that name.

To resolve the disagreement over the baby's name, the family gestured to the mute Zacharias. He asked for a small writing tablet and, to the astonishment of all, wrote the simple sentence: "His name is John." In that very instant, the divine sign was completed. Zacharias’s mouth was opened, his tongue was loosed, and he began to speak, his first words being a joyful hymn of praise and thanksgiving to God for His faithfulness and mercy.

Filled with the Holy Spirit, Zacharias uttered a beautiful prophecy, now known as the Benedictus. He blessed the Lord God of Israel for visiting and redeeming His people and for raising up a horn of salvation in the house of David. He then turned to his infant son and prophesied, “And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare His ways, to give knowledge of salvation to His people.”

Some time after the birth of the Lord Jesus, the wicked King Herod heard of the miraculous birth of John and feared him as a potential rival king. When he commanded the slaughter of the male infants in Bethlehem and the surrounding areas, he also sent soldiers to find and kill the son of Zacharias. The king’s paranoia and cruelty extended beyond Bethlehem, as he sought to eliminate any perceived threat to his throne, especially a child whose birth was accompanied by such wonders.

According to Holy Tradition, when the soldiers arrived, the righteous Elizabeth fled with the infant John into the desert. She cried out to a mountain for help, and a rock miraculously opened to hide them. Enraged that John could not be found, Herod ordered his soldiers to execute Zacharias. The holy priest was slain in the Temple courtyard, between the sanctuary and the altar. His innocent blood spilled upon the marble, where it dried and remained as an indelible witness to Herod’s crime.

The tradition of the Church holds that forty days after the martyrdom of her husband, the righteous Elizabeth also peacefully reposed in the Lord while in the wilderness. The young Saint John, now an orphan, was not left alone. He remained in the desert, protected by God’s divine providence and fed by an angel, growing and becoming strong in spirit until the day he began his public ministry, calling the people of Israel to repentance at the Jordan River.

The Holy Church venerates Zacharias as a Prophet, Priest, and Martyr. He is remembered as the fulfillment of the Old Testament priesthood and the father of the last and greatest of the prophets, Saint John the Forerunner. His steadfastness, culminating in his martyrdom, is honored as a profound act of faith. The Church celebrates the memory of the Holy Prophet Zacharias and the Righteous Elizabeth on September 5, commemorating their pivotal role in the story of our salvation.
